p.src: Now Kongming employed the stratagem of reducing the troops while increasing the cooking fires, and withdrew to Hanzhong; Sima Yi, fearing an ambush, dared not pursue and likewise withdrew his army to Chang'an; thus the Shu army did not lose a single man. After richly rewarding the entire army, Kongming returned to Chengdu, entered the palace to see the Latter Emperor, and memorialized: “This old minister marched from Qishan intending to take Chang'an, but suddenly received Your Majesty's edict recalling me. What grave matter has arisen?” The Latter Emperor had no answer; after a long while he said, “It had been long since We saw the Chancellor's face, and We missed you deeply. Therefore We specially summoned you back; there was no other matter.” Kongming said, “That was not Your Majesty's true intention. Some treacherous minister must have slandered me, saying that I harbored disloyal designs.” Hearing this, the Latter Emperor remained silent and said nothing. Kongming said, “This old minister received profound favor from the Former Emperor and swore to repay it with his life. If there are now treacherous villains within the court, how can I campaign against the enemy?” The Latter Emperor said, “We mistakenly listened to the words of the eunuchs and recalled the Chancellor in a moment of haste. Only today has the obstruction in Our mind been cleared away, but regret comes too late.” Kongming then summoned the eunuchs and questioned them closely, whereupon he learned that Gou An had spread the rumor; he promptly sent men to arrest him, but Gou An had already fled to Wei. Kongming executed the eunuchs who had submitted false reports and expelled all the rest from the palace; he also severely reproached Jiang Wan, Fei Yi, and the others for failing to detect the treachery and admonish the Emperor. The two repeatedly assented and acknowledged their guilt.

p.src: Kongming took leave of the Latter Emperor and returned to Hanzhong. On the one hand, he issued a dispatch ordering Li Yan to furnish provisions and continue transporting them to the front; on the other, he again deliberated on launching a campaign. Yang Yi said, “Our repeated campaigns have exhausted the army, while provisions have repeatedly failed to arrive; it would now be better to divide the troops into two shifts, each serving for three months. If, for example, we have two hundred thousand men, we should lead only one hundred thousand out to Qishan; after they have remained there three months, the other hundred thousand should relieve them. By rotating the two groups in turn, the army's strength will never be depleted. Then, by advancing gradually, we may aspire to conquer the Central Plain.” Kongming said, “These words accord exactly with my own intention. My campaign against the Central Plain is not the work of a single morning or evening; we must indeed make such a long-term plan.” He thereupon issued orders dividing the army into two shifts, each with a term of one hundred days, to rotate in turn; anyone exceeding the appointed term would be punished under military law.

p.src: In the second month of spring in the ninth year of Jianxing, Kongming again led an army against Wei. It was then the fifth year of Taihe in Wei. When Cao Rui, Emperor of Wei, learned that Kongming was again campaigning in the Central Plain, he urgently summoned Sima Yi for counsel. Sima Yi said, “Now that Zidan is dead, I am willing to exert all my strength alone to destroy the rebels and repay Your Majesty.” Cao Rui was delighted and held a banquet in his honor. The next day, a report arrived that the Shu invasion was pressing hard. Cao Rui immediately ordered Sima Yi to take the field against the enemy and personally had the imperial carriage prepared to escort him beyond the city. Taking leave of the Emperor of Wei, Sima Yi went directly to Chang'an, assembled troops from every quarter, and deliberated on a strategy to defeat the Shu army. Zhang He said, “I wish to lead a force to guard Yong and Mei and hold off the Shu army.” Sima Yi said, “My vanguard cannot withstand Kongming's host alone; if we further divide the troops between front and rear, it offers no prospect of victory. It would be better to leave troops to defend Shanggui and send all the rest to Qishan. Would you be willing to serve as vanguard?” Zhang He rejoiced and said, “I have always cherished loyalty and righteousness and wished to devote myself wholly to serving the realm, but regrettably I had never met one who understood me; now that the Commander entrusts me with this heavy duty, I would not refuse though I died ten thousand deaths.” Thereupon Sima Yi appointed Zhang He as vanguard and placed him in overall command of the main army; he also ordered Guo Huai to defend the commanderies of Longxi. The remaining generals advanced by separate routes. Scouts from the vanguard reported: “Kongming is leading his main army toward Qishan. His foremost commanders, Wang Ping and Zhang Yi, have come straight out through Chencang, passed Jiange, and are advancing by way of Sanguan toward Xie Valley.” Sima Yi said to Zhang He, “Now that Kongming is driving deep into our territory, he will surely reap the wheat of Longxi to supply his army. You are to encamp at Qishan, while Guo Huai and I patrol the commanderies around Tianshui to prevent the enemy from harvesting the wheat.” Zhang He accepted the order and led forty thousand troops to defend Qishan. Sima Yi led the main army toward Longxi.

p.src: Now when Kongming's army reached Qishan and had finished making camp, he saw that Wei troops were already prepared along the banks of the Wei River. He therefore said to his generals, “This must be Sima Yi's doing. Our camp is now short of provisions. Though I have repeatedly sent men to press Li Yan to transport rice for our supply, it has still not arrived. I reckon the wheat in Longshang is ripe; we can secretly lead troops to reap it.” He therefore left the four generals Wang Ping, Zhang Yi, Wu Ban, and Wu Yi to guard the camp at Qishan, while he personally led Jiang Wei, Wei Yan, and the other generals onward to Lucheng. The Governor of Lucheng had long known Kongming's reputation and hastily opened the gates and came out to surrender. After reassuring him, Kongming asked, “Where is the wheat ripe at this time?” The Governor replied, “The wheat in Longshang is already ripe.” Kongming then left Zhang Yi and Ma Zhong to guard Lucheng, while he personally led the generals and the entire army toward Longshang. The vanguard returned to report: “Sima Yi is here with his troops.” Kongming exclaimed in surprise, “That man foresaw that I would come to reap the wheat!” He immediately bathed and changed his clothes, then had three identical four-wheeled carriages brought forward, each decorated in precisely the same fashion. These carriages had been built beforehand by Kongming in Shu. Kongming then ordered Jiang Wei to lead one thousand troops in escort of a carriage, with another five hundred beating drums, and to lie in ambush behind Shanggui; Ma Dai on the left and Wei Yan on the right were each likewise to lead one thousand troops escorting a carriage and five hundred troops beating drums. Each carriage was attended by twenty-four men, dressed in black, barefoot, their hair loose and swords in hand; carrying black seven-star banners, they pushed the carriage on either side. Each of the three received his instructions and departed with his troops and carriage. Kongming further ordered thirty thousand troops, each carrying a sickle and pack ropes, to stand ready to harvest the wheat. He then selected twenty-four strong and vigorous men, dressed each in black with loose hair and swords in hand, to cluster around a four-wheeled carriage as its pushers. He ordered Guan Xing to attire himself in the likeness of the celestial general Tianpeng, carrying a black seven-star banner and walking before the carriage. Kongming sat upright upon it and proceeded toward the Wei camp.

p.src: When the scouts saw this, they were greatly alarmed, unable to tell whether these were men or ghosts, and rushed to report to Sima Yi. Sima Yi came out of camp to see for himself. There sat Kongming upright upon the carriage, wearing his headdress and crane-feather cloak and gently waving a feather fan; to either side were twenty-four men with loose hair and swords in hand; and before him walked a man carrying a black banner. In the dim distance, they looked like heavenly spirits. Sima Yi said, “This is another of Kongming's sorceries!” He detached two thousand troops and instructed them: “Hurry after them and seize the carriage and every man with it!” The Wei troops obeyed and charged after them as one. Seeing the Wei troops in pursuit, Kongming ordered the carriage turned and moved slowly toward the Shu camp in the distance. The Wei soldiers all spurred their horses in pursuit, but a chill wind sighed and cold mist spread everywhere. After pursuing with all their strength for some distance but failing to overtake him, they were all greatly alarmed. Reining in their horses, they said, “How strange! We have raced after him for thirty li, yet although he remains visible ahead, we cannot catch him. What are we to do?”

p.src: Seeing that the troops did not approach, Kongming again had his carriage pushed forward and halted facing the Wei soldiers. After hesitating for a long while, the Wei soldiers spurred their horses in pursuit once more. Kongming turned his carriage around again and proceeded slowly. The Wei soldiers pursued for another twenty li, but though they could see him ahead, they could not catch him, and all were left utterly bewildered. Kongming ordered the carriage turned to face the Wei soldiers and had it pushed backward. The Wei soldiers were about to pursue again. Then Sima Yi arrived from the rear at the head of another force. He issued an order: “Kongming is well versed in the Eight Gates and the arts of concealment and can command the spirits of the Six Ding and Six Jia. This is the art of ‘contracting the earth’ from the Celestial Book of the Six Jia. No one is to pursue him.” Just as the soldiers reined in and turned back, war drums thundered on their left and a body of troops charged upon them; Sima Yi hastily ordered his men to resist. From among the Shu ranks appeared twenty-four men with loose hair and swords in hand, dressed in black and barefoot, escorting a four-wheeled carriage. Kongming sat upright upon it, wearing his cap and crane-feather cloak and waving a feather fan in his hand. Sima Yi cried in astonishment, “Just now Kongming was sitting in that other carriage. We pursued him for fifty li without catching him—how can there be another Kongming here? How strange! How strange!” Before he had finished speaking, war drums sounded again on the right and another body of troops charged forth; on their four-wheeled carriage sat yet another Kongming. Beside it were likewise twenty-four men, dressed in black and barefoot, with loose hair and swords in hand, escorting the carriage toward them. Deeply perplexed, Sima Yi looked back at his officers and said, “These must surely be divine troops!” The whole army fell into confusion and, not daring to fight, fled in all directions.

p.src: As they were fleeing, drums suddenly thundered and yet another body of troops attacked. At their head was a four-wheeled carriage upon which Kongming sat erect, with attendants pushing it on either side exactly like those before. Every Wei soldier was horrified. Sima Yi could not tell whether these were men or ghosts, nor how many Shu troops there were. Utterly terrified, he hastily led his army into Shanggui and shut the gates, refusing to emerge. By then Kongming had already ordered thirty thousand picked troops to reap all the wheat in Longshang and transport it to Lucheng for threshing and drying. Sima Yi remained inside Shanggui for three days, not daring to leave the city. Only after he saw the Shu troops withdraw did he dare send soldiers out to reconnoiter. On the road they captured a Shu soldier and brought him before Sima Yi. Sima Yi questioned him. The man replied, “I was one of those reaping the wheat. I lost my horse and was captured and brought here.” Sima Yi asked, “What were those divine troops we saw earlier?” He answered, “The three ambushing forces were not led by Kongming at all, but by Jiang Wei, Ma Dai, and Wei Yan. Each force had only one thousand soldiers escorting the carriage and five hundred beating the drums. Only the man in the carriage that first came to lure your formation was truly Kongming.” Sima Yi raised his face to heaven and sighed deeply: “Kongming possesses the cunning to appear like a god and vanish like a ghost!” Suddenly it was reported that Deputy Commander Guo Huai had come to see him. Sima Yi received him, and after the formal greetings were concluded, Guo Huai said, “I hear that the Shu troops are few and are now threshing wheat at Lucheng. We can attack them.” Sima Yi recounted the earlier events in detail. Guo Huai laughed and said, “That deception could succeed only for a moment. Now that we have seen through it, what is there to fear? I shall lead one force against their rear, while you lead another against their front. Lucheng can be taken and Kongming captured.” Sima Yi agreed, and they came on with their troops divided into two forces.

p.src: Meanwhile, Kongming was leading his army in threshing and drying wheat at Lucheng when he suddenly summoned his officers and gave his orders: “The enemy will certainly attack the city tonight. I judge that the wheat fields east and west of Lucheng offer ample ground for ambushes. Who dares undertake this for me?” The four officers Jiang Wei, Wei Yan, Ma Dai, and Ma Zhong stepped forward and said, “We are willing to go.” Kongming was delighted. He ordered Jiang Wei and Wei Yan each to take two thousand men and lie in ambush to the southeast and northwest respectively. Ma Dai and Ma Zhong were each to take two thousand men and lie in ambush to the southwest and northeast: “When you hear the signal cannon, attack from all four corners at once.” The four officers accepted the plan and departed with their troops. Kongming himself led a little over a hundred men, each carrying firecrackers, out of the city and lay waiting in the wheat fields.

p.src: Now Sima Yi led his troops straight to the foot of Lucheng. Darkness had already fallen, and he said to his officers, “If we advance by daylight, those inside the city will certainly be prepared. We should take advantage of the night to attack. The walls here are low and the moat shallow, so we can readily break through.” He then stationed his troops outside the city. At the first watch, Guo Huai also arrived with his troops. The two forces joined, and at a single roll of the drums they encircled Lucheng as tightly as an iron barrel. From the walls ten thousand crossbows loosed at once, and arrows and stones fell like rain, so the Wei troops dared not advance. Suddenly signal explosions sounded in rapid succession within the Wei army. The whole force was alarmed, not knowing whence the enemy might come. When Guo Huai sent men to search the wheat fields, flames shot skyward at all four corners and battle cries thundered as four Shu forces attacked together. All four gates of Lucheng opened wide and the troops inside charged out. Attacked from within and without, the Wei army was savagely routed, with countless men slain. Sima Yi led the defeated remnants in a desperate charge through the encirclement and occupied a hilltop. Guo Huai likewise led his defeated troops behind the mountain and established a camp there. Kongming entered the city and ordered the four officers to establish camps at the four corners.

p.src: Guo Huai said to Sima Yi, “We have faced the Shu troops for a long time and have found no means of forcing them to retreat. Now we have suffered another defeat and lost more than three thousand men. Unless we devise a plan soon, it will be difficult for us to withdraw later.” Sima Yi asked, “What then should we do?” Guo Huai replied, “We can issue dispatches summoning the troops of Yong and Liang to combine their strength and destroy the enemy. I am willing to lead a force in a surprise attack on Jiange, severing their road home and cutting off their provisions, so that their whole army falls into disorder. Then, if we strike with the advantage of the moment, the enemy can be annihilated.” Sima Yi agreed and at once sent dispatches by night to Yong and Liang, ordering troops to be mobilized. Within a few days, the general Sun Li arrived with troops from the various commanderies. Sima Yi immediately ordered Sun Li to rendezvous with Guo Huai and make a surprise attack on Jiange.

First, they expect our wheat to run out and leave us without provisions. Second, they have sent troops to raid Jiange and cut our supply route. Each of you is to lead ten thousand men ahead and hold the strategic passes. When the Wei troops see that preparations have been made, they will withdraw of their own accord.” The two men departed with their troops. That term has now expired, and the troops from Hanzhong have already emerged from the passes of Shu. The official dispatch from the road ahead has arrived, and they are only waiting to rendezvous and exchange duties. Of the eighty thousand troops now present, forty thousand are due to be relieved.” Kongming said, “Since the order has already been given, have them depart at once.”

p.src: When the soldiers heard the news, each made ready and prepared to depart. Suddenly a report came that Sun Li was leading two hundred thousand troops from Yong and Liang to reinforce the battle and seize Jiange, while Sima Yi himself had brought an army to attack Lucheng. Every man in the Shu army was alarmed. Yang Yi went in and said to Kongming, “The Wei army is advancing with great urgency. Your Excellency should keep back the troops due for relief to repel the enemy, then release them when the fresh troops arrive.” Kongming said, “That cannot be done. In employing soldiers and appointing commanders, I take good faith as the foundation. Since the order was given beforehand, how could I break my word? Moreover, all the Shu soldiers due to leave have prepared for their journey home, while their parents, wives, and children lean against the doors awaiting them. Even if I now faced the gravest peril, I would never detain them.” He immediately issued an order that all troops due to leave should depart that very day. When the soldiers heard it, they all cried aloud, “Since the Prime Minister shows us such kindness, we are willing to remain instead of returning. We shall cast aside our lives and slaughter the Wei troops to repay Your Excellency!” Kongming said, “You ought to return home. How could you remain here any longer?” But all the soldiers wished to fight and refused to go home. Kongming said, “Since you insist on fighting at my side, go outside the city and make camp. When the Wei army arrives, give them no time to catch their breath, but attack at once. This is the method of awaiting the weary in ease.” The soldiers received the order, took up their weapons, and joyfully marched out of the city to form ranks and wait.

I cannot tell what they intend.” Sima Yi said, “Kongming has countless cunning schemes. We must not move rashly. It is better to hold fast. When his provisions are exhausted, he will withdraw of his own accord.” The general Wei Ping stepped forward and said, “The Shu army has struck camp at Qishan and retreated. This is precisely the time to pursue them in the flush of victory. If the Commander keeps the troops motionless and fears Shu like a tiger, what will you do when all the realm laughs at you?” Sima Yi held firmly to his decision and would not consent.

p.src: Now when Kongming learned that the Qishan troops had returned, he summoned Ma Zhong and Yang Yi to his tent and entrusted them with a secret plan. He ordered them to lead ten thousand crossbowmen ahead to the Mumen Road at Jiange and lie in ambush on both sides. “If the Wei troops pursue us there, wait for my cannon signal, then quickly roll down timber and stones to cut off their retreat, and shoot at them from both sides at once.” The two men led their troops away. He then summoned Wei Yan and Guan Xing and ordered them to command the rear guard. Banners were planted all around the walls, while firewood and grass were heaped haphazardly within the city and smoke was raised as a feint. The main army then withdrew toward the Mumen Road.

p.src: A patrol from the Wei camp reported to Sima Yi, “The main body of the Shu army has withdrawn, but we do not know how many troops remain in the city.” Sima Yi went to inspect it himself. Seeing banners on the walls and smoke rising within, he laughed and said, “This is an empty city.” He sent men to investigate, and it was indeed an empty city. Sima Yi was delighted and said, “Kongming has withdrawn. Who dares pursue him?” The vanguard commander Zhang He said, “I am willing to go.” Sima Yi restrained him, saying, “You are impetuous by nature. You must not go.” Zhang He said, “When the Commander marched beyond the pass, you appointed me vanguard. Today is the very moment to win merit, yet you will not employ me. Why?” Sima Yi said, “As the Shu army withdraws, it is sure to have laid ambushes at dangerous passes. Only with the utmost caution may you pursue.” Zhang He said, “I understand already. You need not worry.” Sima Yi said, “Since you insist on going, see that you do not regret it.” Zhang He said, “A true man sacrifices himself to repay his country; though I died ten thousand deaths, I would have no regret.” Sima Yi said, “Since you are resolved to go, you may lead five thousand troops in advance. I shall order Wei Ping to follow with twenty thousand horse and foot to guard against ambush. I myself will lead three thousand troops behind them in support.”

p.src: Zhang He received the order and led his troops in swift pursuit. After traveling more than thirty li, he suddenly heard a tremendous battle cry behind him. A body of troops burst from the woods, and their leading general reined in his horse with saber held crosswise and shouted, “Rebel general, where are you taking those troops?” Zhang He looked back and saw that it was Wei Yan. Enraged, Zhang He wheeled his horse and engaged him. Before ten bouts had passed, Wei Yan feigned defeat and fled. Zhang He pursued for another thirty li or more, then reined in and looked back. Seeing no ambush whatever, he spurred forward again in pursuit. Just as he rounded a hillside, another great cry suddenly arose and a body of troops burst forth. Their leading general was Guan Xing, who reined in his horse with saber held crosswise and shouted, “Zhang He, do not flee! I am here!” Zhang He urged his horse forward and engaged him. Before ten bouts had passed, Guan Xing turned his horse and fled. Zhang He pursued close behind. When they reached a dense wood, Zhang He grew suspicious and sent scouts in every direction, but there was no ambush. Reassured, he resumed the pursuit. Unexpectedly, Wei Yan had circled around ahead of him. Zhang He fought him for more than ten bouts. Wei Yan again fled in defeat. Zhang He pursued in fury, only for Guan Xing to circle ahead and block his way. Zhang He was enraged and spurred his horse into combat. After some ten bouts, the Shu troops abandoned clothing, armor, equipment, and other articles until the road was choked with them. The Wei soldiers all dismounted and scrambled to seize them.

p.src: The two generals, Wei Yan and Guan Xing, took turns engaging the enemy. Zhang He pursued with fierce courage. As night approached, they reached the entrance to the Mumen Road. Wei Yan wheeled his horse and shouted abuse at the top of his voice: “Zhang He, traitorous villain! I will flee from you no longer! Keep coming after me, and now I shall fight you to the death!” Furious beyond measure, Zhang He leveled his spear, drove his horse forward, and charged straight at Wei Yan. Wei Yan swung his saber and met him. Before ten bouts had passed, Wei Yan suffered a crushing defeat. Abandoning clothing, armor, helmet, and even his horse, he led his routed troops into the Mumen Road. Zhang He's bloodlust was aroused, and when he saw Wei Yan fleeing in utter defeat, he spurred his horse after him. By then darkness had fallen. At the blast of a cannon, flames soared skyward from the hills, and great stones and tangled timber came rolling down, blocking the way ahead. Zhang He cried in alarm, “I have fallen into a trap!” When he hastily turned his horse, he found that timber and stones had already choked the road behind. There was only a stretch of open ground between sheer cliffs on either side, and Zhang He had no way forward or back. Suddenly a wooden clapper sounded, and ten thousand crossbows loosed from both sides at once, shooting Zhang He and more than a hundred of his subordinate officers dead in the Mumen Road. p.src: Now Zhang He was dead. When the pursuing Wei troops arrived and found the road blocked, they knew that Zhang He had fallen into a trap. The soldiers reined their horses around and hastily withdrew. Suddenly, a great shout rang out from the mountaintop: “Prime Minister Zhuge is here!” The soldiers looked up and saw Kongming standing amid the firelight. Pointing at them, he said, “Today I went hunting, intending to shoot a ‘horse,’ but by mistake I struck a ‘roebuck.’ Go in peace, every one of you, and report to Zhongda that sooner or later he will surely be captured by me.” The Wei troops returned to Sima Yi and gave him a detailed account of what had happened. Overcome with grief, Yi looked up to Heaven and sighed, “Zhang Junyi’s death is my fault!” He then withdrew his army to Luoyang. When the Ruler of Wei heard of Zhang He’s death, he shed tears and sighed. He ordered that the body be recovered and buried with full honors.

p.src: Meanwhile, Kongming entered Hanzhong and intended to return to Chengdu to see the Latter Emperor. Li Yan, the Protector-General, falsely memorialized the Latter Emperor: “I have already prepared the army’s provisions, and they are about to be transported to the prime minister’s camp. I do not know why the prime minister suddenly withdrew his army.” Upon hearing this memorial, the Latter Emperor at once ordered Imperial Secretary Fei Yi to go to Hanzhong, meet Kongming, and ask why he had withdrawn. Fei Yi reached Hanzhong and conveyed the Latter Emperor’s wishes. Kongming was greatly startled and said, “Li Yan sent me an urgent dispatch saying that Eastern Wu was about to raise an army and invade Shu. That is why I withdrew.” Fei Yi said, “Li Yan memorialized that the provisions were ready and that the prime minister had withdrawn without cause. It was for this reason that His Majesty sent me to inquire.” Kongming flew into a rage and ordered an investigation. It emerged that Li Yan, unable to maintain the army’s supply of provisions and fearing punishment from the prime minister, had sent the dispatch to make him return; he had then falsely memorialized the Emperor to conceal his own failure. Kongming angrily declared, “For his own selfish ends, that wretch has ruined a great affair of state!” He ordered Li Yan summoned and intended to execute him. Fei Yi advised him, “Prime Minister, remember the late Emperor’s charge when he entrusted the orphaned heir to you, and pardon Li Yan for the time being.” Kongming accepted his counsel. Fei Yi then prepared a memorial and reported the matter to the Emperor. After reading the memorial, the Latter Emperor erupted in fury and commanded his guards to drag Li Yan out and behead him. Jiang Wan, an Army Adviser, stepped from the ranks and memorialized, “Li Yan was one of the ministers to whom the late Emperor entrusted the orphaned heir. I beg Your Majesty to show mercy and pardon him.” The Latter Emperor agreed. He immediately demoted Li Yan to commoner status and exiled him to Zitong Commandery, where he was to live in retirement.

p.src: Kongming returned to Chengdu and appointed Li Yan’s son, Li Feng, as Chief Clerk; he gathered fodder and stockpiled grain, instructed his officers in formations and warfare, put military equipment in order, and cared for his commanders and soldiers. Only after three years would he campaign again. The people and soldiers of the Two Riverlands all revered him for his benevolence and virtue. Time slipped swiftly by, and before anyone knew it, three years had passed. It was then the second month of spring in the twelfth year of Jianxing. Kongming entered the court and memorialized, “I have now spent three years caring for the soldiers. Our provisions and fodder are abundant, our military equipment is complete, and our men and horses are strong. We can now campaign against Wei. If this time I do not sweep away the treacherous faction and restore the Central Plains, I swear never to appear before Your Majesty again!” The Latter Emperor said, “The realm now stands divided among three powers, and neither Wu nor Wei has invaded us. Father Chancellor, why not peacefully enjoy this age of tranquility?” Kongming replied, “I received the late Emperor’s grace in recognizing my worth, and even in my dreams I have never ceased devising plans to attack Wei. It is my desire to exert all my strength and fulfill my loyalty, to recover the Central Plains for Your Majesty, and to restore the House of Han.” Before he had finished speaking, a man among the court ranks stepped forward and said, “The prime minister must not raise an army.” All looked toward him: it was Qiao Zhou.
